title: Glory on the Mountain, Need in the Valley
summary: On a high mountain Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James, and John, Moses and Elijah appear with him, and a voice from the cloud declares him God's beloved Son. Coming down, Jesus identifies John the Baptist as the promised Elijah, heals a boy the disciples could not help, and teaches them about faith. He predicts his death a second time, and in Capernaum he provides the temple tax through a coin found in a fish's mouth.
story: Six days after Peter's confession and Jesus' first prediction of his death, three disciples see his glory. The order matters. Jesus has just said that the road to his kingdom runs through suffering; now the Father confirms that the one who will suffer is his beloved Son. The chapter then descends from the mountain into a valley of failure and need: a suffering boy, disciples with too little faith, a second passion prediction that grieves them. The glory is real, but it does not remove the cross. The closing story about the temple tax, found only in Matthew, raises the question of how the Son of God relates to the institutions of Israel, a question that will grow sharper when he reaches Jerusalem.
historical:
Matthew does not name the mountain. Christian tradition, from at least the fourth century, identified it with Mount Tabor in lower Galilee, while many modern scholars suggest Mount Hermon, which rises above Caesarea Philippi where the previous scene took place. Either is possible, and the text is more interested in the mountain's echo of Sinai than in its location. Mark 9:2-29 and Luke 9:28-43 tell the transfiguration and the healing of the boy, and 2 Peter 1:16-18 recalls the voice heard on the holy mountain.

The two-drachma tax was the annual temple tax that Jewish men paid for the upkeep of the temple's worship, based on the half-shekel of Exodus 30:11-16. Jews throughout the Roman world sent it to Jerusalem. After the temple was destroyed in AD 70, the emperor Vespasian redirected the tax to the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus in Rome, which would have given this story fresh relevance for Matthew's first readers if the Gospel was written after that date. The coin in verse 27 is a stater, worth four drachmas, exactly enough for two people. Verse 21, which appears in later manuscripts (saying that this kind goes out only by prayer and fasting), is missing from the earliest ones and was probably added from Mark 9:29.
cultural:
Moses and Elijah were the great figures of Israel's law and prophets. Both met God on a mountain (Sinai, also called Horeb), both had endings that later Jewish tradition surrounded with mystery (Deuteronomy 34:6; 2 Kings 2:11), and Malachi 4:4-6 names them together at the close of the prophets, promising that Elijah would come before the great day of the Lord. That is why the scribes taught that Elijah must come first. Peter's offer of three shelters (skene, tent or booth) may recall the Feast of Tabernacles, when Israelites lived in booths to remember God's care in the wilderness, and when some hoped the Messiah would appear. A bright cloud recalls the cloud of God's glory that covered Sinai and filled the tabernacle.

The boy's father uses a word (selēniazomai) that literally means to be moonstruck, reflecting an ancient belief that the moon caused seizures, and the symptoms he describes are those modern medicine calls epilepsy. Matthew also says a demon was involved. Mustard seed was proverbial for smallness, and moving mountains was a Jewish figure of speech for doing what seems impossible. Kings in the ancient world taxed conquered peoples, not their own families, which gives Jesus' question to Peter its point.
literary: The chapter falls into four scenes. The transfiguration (verses 1 to 8) is told with deliberate echoes of Moses on Sinai in Exodus 24 and 34: a high mountain, a period of six days, a cloud, a voice, and a shining face. The conversation on the way down (verses 9 to 13) connects glory and suffering: as Elijah (John) suffered, so will the Son of Man. The healing (verses 14 to 20) contrasts the mountain with the valley, much as Moses came down from Sinai to find Israel failing. The second passion prediction (verses 22 and 23) and the temple tax (verses 24 to 27) close the chapter with Jesus as both the suffering Son of Man and the royal Son who is free, yet chooses not to give offense. The Father's words in verse 5 repeat the voice at Jesus' baptism (3:17) and add “Listen to Him!”

outline.t: A boy healed; the power of faith
The second prediction of death and resurrection
The temple tax and the coin in the fish

doctrines.note: The transfiguration reveals Jesus' true glory for a moment and the Father names him beloved Son. Moses and Elijah talk with him and then disappear, leaving Jesus alone: the law and the prophets point to him, and the command is now to listen to him.

As at the baptism, the Father speaks from heaven of the Son. The Son's glory shines from within him, not reflected from outside, as Moses' face reflected God's glory. The church has seen here a glimpse of the Son's divine nature veiled in his humanity.
The disciples fail not for lack of technique but for little faith. Jesus teaches that even faith as small as a mustard seed, because it rests on God's power, can do what seems impossible.

words.note: Metamorphoo, to be transformed or changed in form. Jesus' appearance changes as his glory becomes visible. Paul uses the same verb for believers being changed into Christ's image (2 Corinthians 3:18) and for being transformed by the renewing of the mind (Romans 12:2).

Oligopistia, littleness of faith, found only here in the New Testament. It is the noun form of Matthew's favorite description of the disciples, of little faith. Jesus' diagnosis is not that they have no faith, but that it is too small, and even small faith rightly placed is enough.

Didrachmon, a two-drachma coin, the amount of the annual temple tax. Since the coin was not commonly minted in this period, the tax was often paid in larger coins such as the Tyrian shekel, worth four drachmas, which could cover two people, as the stater in verse 27 does.

Skene, tent or shelter. The word recalls the tabernacle, God's tent among Israel in the wilderness, and the booths of the Feast of Tabernacles. Peter's wish to build shelters may be an attempt to hold the glorious moment in place, but the cloud and the voice interrupt him.

christ: The transfiguration is a preview of Jesus' glory as the risen and coming Son of Man, promised in 16:27-28. Where Moses' face shone because he had been with God, Jesus' face shines like the sun from within. The Father's words combine Psalm 2:7 (the royal Son), Isaiah 42:1 (the Servant in whom God delights), and Deuteronomy 18:15, where Moses promised that God would raise up a prophet like him and said Israel must listen to him. Jesus is king, servant, and prophet at once. Coming down, he links his glory with the suffering already inflicted on John and soon to be inflicted on him. In the tax scene he speaks as the Son of the King whose house the temple is, free from its tax, yet paying it so as not to offend, the same humility that will take him to the cross.

hard.q: Was the boy suffering from epilepsy or from a demon, and how should modern readers take the Gospels' accounts of possession?
hard.a: The father's description (seizures, falling into fire and water) matches what we now call epilepsy, and Matthew uses a word that reflects ancient ideas about the moon. Yet he also says Jesus rebuked a demon that came out of the boy. Readers respond in different ways. Some take possession as the ancient explanation for what we now understand as medical conditions, and read Jesus' healing as compassion expressed in the categories of his time. Others hold that the Gospels describe real spiritual oppression that may produce physical symptoms, noting that the Gospels themselves distinguish between ordinary illness and possession (as in 4:24, which lists the demon-possessed and those with seizures separately). Many Christians hold both: that epilepsy is a medical condition and should never in itself be attributed to demons, and that the Gospels bear witness to real evil powers that Jesus defeated. What should not follow from this passage is any suggestion that people with epilepsy or mental illness today are possessed. The Gospel's own focus is on Jesus' compassion, his authority over whatever held the boy, and the disciples' need for faith.

questions: The disciples were told “Listen to Him!” What voices compete with Jesus' for your attention, and how do you listen to him?
After the mountaintop came the valley of need. How do moments of seeing God clearly prepare you for ordinary days of struggle?
Jesus paid a tax he did not owe so as not to cause offense. Where might you set aside a right you have for the sake of others?
